title: Router-lookahead prefetch pages MoE experts from flash
idea: IFR: only the experts this token uses occupy memory. Closest: a small predictor reads layer-i hidden states to guess the top experts for layers i+1 to i+3 and prefetches them from flash into an expert cache; a miss falls back to the always-resident shared expert for that token.
why: Large MoE serving keeps only 10-20% expert residency, cutting DRAM 5-8x.

title: Liver-style compensatory compression covers modules out for repair
idea: The liver regrows mass to keep function after losing tissue; when modules are pulled for repair the memory manager raises compression levels on the remaining DRAM to hold logical capacity constant, then relaxes it after reinsertion, so maintenance never shrinks jobs.
why: Removes 5-10% maintenance headroom and makes hot repair routine.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM holding year-frozen foundation model weights
idea: A standard base die, built on a DRAM-periphery or mature logic process, adds one contact/via mask that encodes a frozen model's weights as present or absent vias. Each bit takes about 2-4 F^2 and needs no capacitor and no refresh. The dies stack HBM-style beside the accelerator, and each new model release costs just that one mask. The time-scale insight: weights stay unchanged for 6-18 months, so they need no rewritable cells.
why: Weights (30-60% of inference HBM) leave DRAM entirely. A ROM bit costs about 3x less than a DRAM bit and needs no refresh energy, all for one added mask per model version.

title: Glass-interposer LPDDR fan-out replaces HBM stacks
idea: IFR: bandwidth without the TSV tax. The constraint drives toward Si/Al/O/Na/Ca glass: aluminosilicate glass interposers with fine Cu/Ti redistribution wiring fan out 16-32 standard LPDDR dies around the accelerator at wide I/O, with no TSVs and no Ta barriers.
why: HBM uses ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR (fact 6); delivering similar capacity with planar LPDDR needs about one third of the DRAM wafers.

title: NAND-resident KV cache with in-flash top-k selection
idea: Worsen: keep the whole multi-million-token KV cache in HBM. Flip: put KV on NAND and give each flash die a tiny dot-product engine that scores keys against the query in place, returning only the top 1% of KV pairs to the GPU for exact attention.
why: Cost: KV at about $0.05/GB in flash vs HBM at about $20/GB, so 100-400x; trades approximate (top-k) attention and higher latency.

title: Memory-efficient device certification with per-GB-avoided credits
idea: Box: demand reallocation × consumer OS and procurement × device SKU × certification × zram + app freeze-to-flash + shared web engine. Phones and laptops that pass a responsiveness benchmark with less DRAM earn a label and a per-GB-avoided credit funded by datacenter buyers.
why: Consumer devices take roughly half of DRAM bits; a 25% trim there frees ~10% of world supply for servers without building anything, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Jacquard punch cards: via-programmed ROM stores frozen base model
idea: A loom's pattern is punched holes: freeze a foundation model's weights into mask-ROM where one cheap via mask (no EUV, back-end only, <=400 C) programs every bit, stacked in 2-4 back-end crosspoint layers on a logic chip; fine-tunes and LoRA deltas stay in DRAM.
why: ROM is denser, refresh-free and capex-light versus DRAM; for million-unit edge/inference SKUs base-weight DRAM goes to zero.

title: One cache only: merge the database buffer pool with page cache
idea: Po: there is only one cache in the machine. A kernel interface lets databases and storage engines adopt the OS page cache as their buffer pool, with app-controlled eviction hints and pinning, eliminating the second copy of every hot page on U.S.-made servers.
why: Double caching wastes up to 2x on hot data; unifying recovers 20-40% of DRAM in storage-heavy servers.

title: Discounted compressed-memory instance tier sold to tenants
idea: Combine cloud billing with transparent zswap/controller compression: sell instances priced per logical GB at a discount where the provider backs part of the memory with compressed pages, and expose per-tenant compression stats so customers restructure data to compress better.
why: Aligns price signals with compressibility; a 1.5-2x fleet effective-capacity gain means fewer DRAM bits purchased.

title: Table-side hot pot: attention cooked inside the memory module
idea: Like hot pot where diners cook at the table instead of the kitchen, put decode-attention units inside commodity LPDDR CXL modules so the KV cache never leaves them; the GPU sends the query vector and receives the attention output.
why: Moves the largest inference memory consumer out of scarce HBM (~3x wafer per bit) into commodity DRAM and cuts decode data-movement energy ~5-10x.

title: Gist tokens compress idle conversation context into learned summaries
idea: Inverts 'context must be kept as raw per-token KV': when a session goes idle, a small trained compressor squeezes its KV into a few dozen 'gist' states that condition the model almost equivalently when the user returns. It is software only and runs on GPUs already installed.
why: Resident KV for idle multi-turn sessions drops 10-50x, so existing hardware can hold far more concurrent users.

title: Seed bank weights: PRNG seeds plus low-rank corrections in NV
idea: Like a seed vault storing seeds instead of forests, store each weight block as a 32-bit PRNG seed selecting a random basis, a few coefficients and a low-rank residual in on-package NV; a hardware LFSR regrows the block in SRAM at compute time.
why: ~3-4 bits per weight-equivalent, zero DRAM for weights, native persistence; trades cheap logic for scarce memory.

title: Family tree: fine-tuned variants stored as 1-bit deltas
idea: Siblings share most genes: serve hundreds of fine-tuned models from one base copy plus per-variant sign-bit deltas with per-row scales, applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel. Software and firmware only, no process step.
why: Serving 100 variants needs ~1.1x base-model memory instead of 100x.

title: Exchange matching engines: keep the input log, replay state on demand
idea: From exchanges that can rebuild any order book from a deterministic input journal: rarely read service state (sessions, carts, per-user caches) is not kept resident; only an append-only input log on flash plus periodic snapshots exist, and state is rebuilt by deterministic replay when a request arrives.
why: For long-tail state touched once every few hours, replay replaces resident bytes, cutting DRAM for that state 10-100x and the water to make it.

title: One hybrid-bond pad mask bolting a compressor onto every bank
idea: A single added Cu hybrid-bond pad mask on top of a standard DRAM wafer exposes each bank's internal data bus. A face-to-face bonded logic die compresses and decompresses per bank at internal bandwidth, so the capacity gain costs no external bandwidth. Compression moves from the CPU, centimeters away, to the bank, micrometers away.
why: About 2x effective capacity at bank-level bandwidth, with no TSVs and one mask.

title: Idle consumer PCs and consoles run offline batch AI jobs
idea: Reverse where batch AI lives: embedding generation, evaluation sweeps and synthetic-data jobs are split into small-model shards and dispatched (Folding@home-style, for paid credits) to idle gaming PCs and consoles whose 16-32 GB of DRAM and GPUs sit unused most hours.
why: Shifts latency-tolerant memory demand off datacenter DRAM onto hundreds of millions of GB already built; no new fab output, so no neon or helium.

title: Functional pages: page-table entries that point to generators
idea: Much DRAM holds data derivable from a short program: hashed embeddings, lookup tables, procedural textures, constant or zero-filled arrays. Add a page-table entry type whose payload is a generator-kernel ID plus parameters; a near-memory engine synthesizes the requested 64 B line on read and caches it in a small buffer, so the bits are never stored.
why: The bound becomes Kolmogorov complexity, not raw size: TB-scale recommender embedding tables could shrink 10-100x through hash-composed embeddings.

title: Cobalt kobold miners: tiny SRAM index picks which KV pages to fetch
idea: Cobalt is named for the kobold that hunted ore; each 16-token KV page gets a 64-byte summary (per-channel key min/max) in SRAM, decode computes upper-bound attention scores from the summaries and fetches only the top 3-5% of pages from DRAM, while the rest of the KV lives in CXL memory or NAND.
why: Per-token KV traffic falls 20-30x (well over 10x lower energy per access), and the HBM/DRAM KV footprint shrinks to the hot pages with the long tail in cheaper flash (energy, cost/bit).

title: Sourdough starter: persist tokens, regrow KV on demand
idea: Keep only the starter: persist each session's token IDs (2-4 bytes per token) to flash and drop its KV cache (100 KB+ per token on large models) under pressure; a cost model chooses between regrowing KV by prefill on idle compute and fetching a stored copy.
why: Persistent state shrinks ~10^4-10^5x per token; exploits compute being more abundant than memory.

title: Intermodal containers: data stays compressed from SSD to SM register
idea: Shipping containers are never unpacked between ship, rail and truck. Define one compressed block format (4 KB blocks of individually indexable 128B compressed lines) that the SSD, NIC, CXL switch, DRAM controller and GPU L2 all understand. Data is then decompressed only into L1 or the register file at the point of use, and stays compressed in DRAM and HBM.
why: Today data is decompressed into DRAM, so compression saves storage, not memory; keeping it compressed in DRAM gives 1.5-3x more HBM/DRAM capacity and bandwidth for weights, KV and tables.

title: Carbon backbone documents: schema skeleton shared, only functional groups stored
idea: Organic molecules share a carbon backbone and differ only in functional groups; an in-memory document store (JSON/protobuf caches, Redis hashes) hash-conses each distinct key-set and type layout once as a backbone, and stores each document as a backbone ID plus a packed value vector, with a shape-lookup instruction so a field access stays one dependent load.
why: Repeated keys, type tags and padding are 40-70% of bytes in JSON-heavy caches; sharing backbones cuts those caches 2-3x in DRAM (cost/bit, density).

title: Gaines stochastic computing: noise-driven rounding removes FP32 master weights
idea: Revive Gaines' 1967 stochastic computing by putting true-random noise sources (university-fabbed avalanche diodes or RTN transistors) in the memory write path, so every weight update into a bf16/fp8 store is stochastically rounded in hardware at no compute cost.
why: Unbiased stochastic rounding lets training drop FP32 master weights and FP32 optimizer copies, ~2-4x less training memory.

title: Copy-on-write base pages plus sparse deltas for full fine-tunes
idea: Combine page-level copy-on-write sharing with delta compression of fully fine-tuned models: each variant is stored as the base model's pages plus sparse, quantized delta pages, and the GPU load path composes base+delta tile by tile into SRAM during GEMM.
why: Serving 50 full fine-tunes costs about one base plus 50 small deltas (each ~5-10% of base) instead of 50 full copies.

title: Dictionary: fleet-trained compression dictionaries pinned per workload
idea: Train zstd-style dictionaries per workload class (JVM heaps, Python objects, embeddings) from fleet samples, ship them signed with the binary, and pin them in the hardware compressor's SRAM so even single 4 KB pages compress against a rich shared context.
why: Small-page ratio rises from ~2x to 3x or more, making zswap/hardware compressed tiers 30-50% more effective at saving DRAM.

title: LLNL ZFP arrays, fixed: lossy compression as a page attribute
idea: ZFP fixed-rate lossy floating-point compression saw low adoption because codes had to be rewritten around compressed-array classes. Put a ZFP engine in the memory controller and let the OS mark pages 'fp64 lossy, 16 bits/value', so unmodified HPC codes get 4x compression with bounded error.
why: ~4x effective DRAM for simulation fields, so HPC nodes need far less DRAM.

title: Minify duplicates: one copy per rack replaces cache tiers
idea: Minify the 6-10 copies a hot byte has in a web stack (Redis/memcached tier, DB buffer pool, OS page cache, replicas): database pages live once in rack-shared, coherent CXL memory that app servers read directly with loads, and the separate cache fleets are retired.
why: Total DRAM per unit of hot data drops ~6-10x, with no new memory technology.

title: Thin-provisioned DRAM die with on-die row indirection
idea: This adds zero masks. A latch-based row indirection table in the periphery lets a die advertise about 1.5x more logical rows than it has physical rows. A physical row is allocated on the first non-zero write, and rows that are freed or zeroed through a TRIM-like command return to the pool. Virtual memory moves down to the die scale.
why: Zero or never-written memory is 10-30% of allocated footprint. Die-level thin provisioning reclaims it transparently, for 1.2-1.4x effective capacity.

title: Oxygen oxidation: line-granular reclamation of dead objects inside live pages
idea: The GC mark phase writes per-64 B-line liveness bits into a controller-held table; lines that have oxidized (dead) inside pages that still hold live objects are released to a line-level free pool and the page is remapped through a sub-page indirection table, so memory returns to the system without moving live objects.
why: Managed heaps hold 20-35% dead-but-unreclaimable space due to page-granular fragmentation; sub-page reclamation recovers most of it, ~1.2-1.4x less DRAM per JVM/Go/JS host (density).

title: Depth-recurrent models reuse one block's weights across time steps
idea: This adds zero masks. Model labs train looped or depth-recurrent transformers that apply a few weight blocks repeatedly across depth, with tiny per-iteration adapters. Space (unique layers) is traded for time (iterations), paid for with compute that decode leaves idle anyway.
why: 4-8x fewer resident weight bytes at similar quality on many tasks, freeing HBM for KV.

title: Setun balanced-ternary cells for native 1.58-bit weights
idea: Revive the 1958 Setun computer's balanced-ternary storage: a university-built crossbar in which each cell holds -1/0/+1 as two complementary ferroelectric states, and the bitline sums currents with sign, so ternary MACs need no multiplier and each weight costs log2(3) bits.
why: Ternary (BitNet-style) models need ~10x less weight memory than fp16; native ternary cells avoid 2-bit padding (26% overhead) and keep weights out of DRAM entirely.

title: Frozen foundation models burned into via-programmed ROM
idea: IFR: weights use no DRAM because they are the hardware. Closest: for models frozen for years (speech, embedding, vision encoders) weights are encoded by one custom via mask as ROM beside the MACs at ~0.1 um2/bit, with LoRA adapters in SRAM for updates.
why: Removes 70-90% of inference DRAM for frozen models; ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and only one non-EUV custom mask.

title: Mature-node fat capacitors enable tri-level DRAM for approximate data
idea: Combine NAND-style multi-level sensing with DRAM on a relaxed DUV node, where larger cells hold enough charge for three levels: a two-step sense amplifier resolves 0/half/1, storing 1.58 bits per cell for error-tolerant data such as activations, low mantissa planes or KV, with a binary mode for everything else.
why: +58% bits per cell without lithographic shrink, turning the absence of EUV (bigger cells, more charge, fact 1) into multi-level margin.

title: Read-mostly tier on legacy SLC NAND for weights and code
idea: Inverts 'working memory needs unlimited endurance': weights, shared libraries and embedding tables are rarely written, so they are mapped byte-addressably onto pSLC NAND from depreciated 2D and early-3D NAND lines. A DRAM read cache sits in front, and a write-rate limiter enforces the endurance budget.
why: Read-mostly bytes are 30-60% of inference memory; moving them to existing NAND frees DRAM at ~1/10 the cost per bit.

title: Chromium palette: weights as indices into base-die SRAM codebooks
idea: Chromium means color; like an indexed-color GIF, each 8-weight vector is stored in DRAM as a 16-bit index into per-layer codebooks held in SRAM on the HBM base die, which expands indices next to the TSVs so DRAM bursts and TSVs carry only indices.
why: About 2 bits per weight moved instead of 16 for bf16 gives ~8x fewer DRAM bits, and with no overfetch of unused precision ~10x lower energy per weight fetched, while weight DRAM shrinks ~8x (energy, density).

title: One-dollar MCU trick: decompress weights inside the MAC pipeline
idea: From $1 microcontrollers that run neural nets from compressed flash: accelerators keep weights entropy-coded (ANS over exponents plus clustered mantissa palettes) in HBM and decode them in a stage fused into each MAC array, so uncompressed weights never exist in memory.
why: Lossless exponent coding saves 25-40% of BF16/FP8 weight bytes and palettes 2-4x, gaining capacity and bandwidth at once.

title: Scandium-doped AlN FeFETs keep weights resident at 125 C
idea: Store weights as polarization states in AlScN ferroelectric FETs, arranged in a NOR array that performs the MAC in place. With a Curie point above 1000 C and a ~4 MV/cm coercive field, the wurtzite polarization does not depolarize over 10 years at 125 C. DRAM holds only activations.
why: Edge and automotive accelerators drop the LPDDR weight copy (often 60-80% of capacity) and avoid the 4x refresh penalty DRAM pays at 125 C.

title: Seed dormancy with cue-triggered germination for cold pages
idea: Cold pages are dried into compact 'seeds' (compressed to ~25%) in a far tier; a tiny learned cue detector watches request streams for germination cues (user login, job phase markers, specific syscalls) and rehydrates exactly those seeds ahead of use, as seeds sprout on temperature and moisture cues rather than on demand.
why: Tiering: lets 40-60% of resident data leave DRAM with fewer demand-miss stalls than recency-based tiering.

title: Card catalog: tiny learned index in DRAM, records in NV
idea: Like a library card catalog pointing into the stacks, keep a piecewise-linear learned index of a few MB in DRAM that predicts the exact NV page holding any key, so each lookup costs one byte-addressable NV read and records never need DRAM residency.
why: Key-value index memory shrinks 10-100x vs DRAM B-trees and data stays durable on CXL-NAND or MRAM.

title: Free in-DRAM row copy unlocks aggressive copy-on-write sharing
idea: In-subarray row copy (RowClone-style back-to-back activation) breaks copy-on-write in about 90 ns instead of a microsecond page copy over the bus. With the time cost of unsharing 10x lower, the OS shares far more aggressively: fork-heavy servers, VM clones, database snapshots, and pages with short expected sharing lifetimes.
why: When unsharing is nearly free in time, sharing pays off even for short-lived pages. That adds 10-30% to dedup savings.

title: CCD bucket-brigade wells store transient activations as analog charge
idea: Write inter-layer activations as analog charge packets into a buried-channel CCD shift register, one packet per value at 5-6 effective bits. The packets are clocked bucket-brigade style to the consuming layer. Activations are consumed within microseconds, so dark-current loss is negligible and neither refresh nor an ADC is needed before use.
why: One ~2F^2 charge well replaces 8-16 DRAM bits per activation, about 4-8x density for transient data (facts 1, 4).

title: Million-token sessions park tokens, regenerate KV on resume
idea: From AI agents with million-token contexts that sit idle most of the time: idle sessions keep only token IDs (2-4 bytes per token) plus sparse anchor-layer KV checkpoints, and the full KV-cache is regenerated by a batched prefill burst on resume, scheduled onto spare compute.
why: KV is 100 KB-1 MB per token versus 4 bytes for the token; parking cuts HBM held by idle sessions 100x+, and HBM (3x wafer area per bit, fact 6) carries the most fab water per bit, so water falls >10x.

title: Floyd-Steinberg dithering for 2-bit KV and activation storage
idea: Borrow error-diffusion halftoning from printing: when quantizing KV vectors to 2 bits, push each token's quantization error into the next token's pre-quantization value so errors cancel in the attention-weighted sum instead of accumulating as bias.
why: Makes ultra-low-bit storage (2 vs 16 bits) usable because attention sums many tokens and diffused error averages out; ~8x KV capacity.

title: Datacenter-wide prefix radix tree deduplicates shared KV across users
idea: IFR: identical context is cached once for the planet. Closest with no materials: a cluster-wide radix tree keyed by token prefixes stores shared KV blocks (system prompts, popular documents, few-shot examples) once per pod, and requests are routed to the pod holding their longest prefix.
why: Shared prefixes are 30-70% of tokens in many products; that share of KV is deduplicated.

title: Hardware concurrent garbage collector lets heaps run near live size
idea: IFR: managed heaps equal their live set. Closest: a GC engine in the memory controller marks and compacts concurrently, with read-barrier forwarding checks in the load path, so runtimes run at 1.1-1.2x live set instead of the 2-3x headroom software GC needs.
why: Java/Go/.NET heaps are a large share of server DRAM and 40-60% of it is headroom; that headroom is removed.

title: Mapmaker's zoom levels: bit-plane tiering of tensors across memory tiers
idea: A mapmaker never prints every street at world scale. Weights and KV are stored transposed into bit-planes: the top 3-4 planes live in HBM and the low-order planes in CXL DRAM or flash. Matmuls run on the coarse planes first and fetch fine planes only for rows whose partial results sit near a decision boundary, such as attention top-k or softmax peaks.
why: Most scores are decided by the MSBs, so HBM capacity per model drops 2-4x and HBM traffic drops roughly in proportion.

title: Kintsugi: OS maps around defects, accepting flawed DRAM dies
idea: Kintsugi makes broken pottery valuable: qualify DIMMs with up to ~1% failing rows, ship each module's defect map in SPD, and have firmware/OS permanently retire those pages at boot; modules are built with standard <260 C reflow only.
why: Turns yield fallout and downbinned dies into sellable capacity, plausibly +3-8% bit supply at zero fab capex.

title: Latent image writes: retention-tuned NV programming for short-lived data
idea: Like exposed-but-undeveloped film, data predicted short-lived is written to NV (SLC NAND, MRAM, ReRAM) with weak fast pulses giving days of retention, enough to survive outages, and is 'developed' with full-strength pulses only if it lives long; a lifetime predictor picks the mode.
why: Lets non-volatile media absorb DRAM-tier write traffic with 3-10x less write energy and wear, shrinking the DRAM tier while staying persistent.

title: Bump-in-the-wire compression ASIC built in 130 nm aluminium fabs
idea: IFR: every DRAM chip holds twice its bits for free. Closest within the constraint: an inline CXL/DIMM LZ-class compressor plus zero-line elider fabbed on 130 nm Al-interconnect lines (Ti/TiN barriers, TiSi2 contacts, no W plugs, no Hf); the OS overcommits physical memory 2x with backpressure when compressibility drops.
why: 2-3x effective capacity per DRAM bit on typical server data, made in idle U.S. mature fabs.

title: Poly-load 4T SRAM, fixed: BEOL oxide-TFT loads atop logic
idea: 1990s 4T SRAM with polysilicon resistor loads was dropped for standby current and poor stability. Replace the resistors with ultra-low-leakage oxide-semiconductor TFT pull-ups stacked in the BEOL directly above the four silicon transistors, so the cell's silicon footprint is ~60% of 6T while static stability returns.
why: ~1.6x denser capacitorless SRAM on logic, enabling bigger on-die buffers that replace DRAM in edge and AI chips.

title: Minify embedding tables to hash encoders plus tiny MLPs
idea: Minify TB-scale recommender embedding tables into multi-hash encoders plus a small MLP that computes each embedding on the fly on tensor cores (deep hash embedding), with no stored rows.
why: Embedding memory falls 100x+, and recommender inference, a top consumer of server DRAM, needs >=10x less of it.

title: Hot-field arenas: garbage collector splits objects so rows carry hot bytes
idea: IFR: every fetched byte gets used. Closest: a managed runtime profiles per-field access and, during compaction, moves hot fields into dense hot arenas in near DRAM and cold fields into a far-memory arena reached by a compressed offset.
why: Objects average 20-40% hot fields; near-tier footprint drops 1.5-2x and row overfetch (fact 8) falls with it.

title: Satellite onboard latents: models compute directly on codec output
idea: From Earth-observation satellites that downlink only learned-codec latents: cameras and NICs emit learned-codec latent tensors and vision/analytics models are trained to consume latents directly, so raw frames are never decoded into DRAM anywhere in the pipeline.
why: Latents are 20-100x smaller than raw frames, so per-stream DRAM falls 20x+ and the embedded fab ultrapure water for those bits falls proportionally (>10x).

title: Minify resident weights to a 3-layer ring streamed from NAND
idea: Minify weight residency to a ring buffer of 2-3 layers: weights stream from a 64-channel NAND array at >=100 GB/s per accelerator while large-batch compute hides the streaming time, layer by layer.
why: DRAM for weights drops 10-40x, and NAND bits cost ~1/15 of DRAM. Capacity per dollar rises >=10x at roughly equal system cost.

title: DRAM test-mode compare reused as in-chip dedup verifier
idea: This adds zero masks. The parallel-test compare circuitry that already sits on every DRAM die for production test is exposed as a runtime command. A candidate duplicate page is then verified bit-exact inside the DRAM in one operation, instead of streaming both copies to the CPU. A factory-time feature becomes a runtime one.
why: It removes the 2 x 4 KB of bandwidth and energy each dedup verification costs, which makes continuous fine-grained dedup cheap: 10-25% capacity savings on VM hosts.

title: Store KV cache as token IDs plus sparse anchors
idea: A token is ~17 bits of information, but its KV cache in a 70B-class model is ~160-320 KB, an expansion of ~100,000x. Keep only token IDs and a full KV snapshot every 64 tokens (anchors); on access, regenerate the missing span's KV with a batched prefill from the nearest anchor on tensor cores that sit idle during memory-bound decode.
why: KV capacity falls ~30-60x for long contexts and parked sessions. The price is ~1.2-2x extra prefill FLOPs, paid from compute that is otherwise stranded.

title: Genome Project biologist: open atlas of real memory contents
idea: Biology took off once the genome was sequenced. An opt-in agent samples hashed, entropy-profiled page snapshots (never raw data) from volunteer fleets and publishes a 'memory atlas': the share of zero pages, duplicates, near-duplicates, compressible types, pointer density and cold data by workload. About $800k.
why: Outside three hyperscalers, nobody knows where the reclaimable bytes are. The atlas aims every compression, dedup and tiering effort at the biggest wins, priming 20-40% savings.

title: Galvanizing: structure plated with protection, payload left raw
idea: Galvanizing coats only the surface of steel with zinc. A type-annotated allocator puts pointers, lengths, keys, headers and control state in ECC-protected memory, and bulky approximate payloads (images, embeddings, audio, ML features, KV values) in 1%-BER cells. Compiler-checked 'approximate' qualifiers stop raw data from flowing into addresses or branches.
why: Payload is 80-95% of the bytes in ML feature stores, media caches and key-value stores, so moving it to cheap tolerant cells cuts premium DRAM 5-10x.

title: Minify graphs with gap-coded adjacency and hardware decoder
idea: Minify web and social graph adjacency using WebGraph-style reference copying, gap and zeta coding. A near-memory decoder streams neighbor lists at line rate to the graph engine.
why: Graph analytics needs 10-20x less memory per edge, so trillion-edge graphs fit in one rack.

title: Swap HBM-resident MoE experts for host-DDR experts with lookahead gating
idea: Substitute 'all experts resident' with 'experts on call'. All experts sit in standard host DDR5 with a hot-expert cache in HBM; a tiny predictor applies the next layer's router to the current hidden state, so the needed experts are DMA'd over existing PCIe/NVLink one layer ahead.
why: MoE models activate ~5-10% of experts per token. HBM holding 20-30% of expert weights cuts HBM per model 3-4x and moves the rest to cheaper DDR bits.

title: Tera MTA, fixed: barrel-threaded cores running graphs from flash
idea: Tera/Cray XMT hid memory latency with 128 hardware threads per core but lost on single-thread performance. Put XMT-style barrel cores (thousands of threads, SRAM register files) inside an SSD controller so graph analytics run directly against NAND's ~20 us reads, with throughput coming from concurrency instead of DRAM.
why: Trillion-edge graphs run without TB-scale DRAM on ~10-20x cheaper-per-bit NAND.

title: Retired FPGA SmartNICs host retired DDR4 as memory expanders
idea: Box: reuse × decommissioned FPGA boards × DIMM × redeployment × PCIe-attached memory-controller bitstream. Retired FPGA cards are reprogrammed as memory controllers for tested DDR4 RDIMMs harvested from retired servers and exposed as a warm tier for page cache and KV spill.
why: Both parts already exist: zero new wafer starts and so zero new fluorinated chemistry, while a near-free warm tier absorbs 20–30% of a host's capacity demand.

title: Graphcore IPU, fixed: hybrid-bonded MRAM weight die under SRAM
idea: Graphcore's SRAM-only IPU faded because 900 MB on-chip could not hold modern models and its DDR streaming was slow. Hybrid-bond a read-optimized STT-MRAM die (weights are written rarely, so slow high-energy writes and limited endurance do not matter) directly under the compute die at >10 TB/s.
why: Gigabytes of weights per package with no DRAM or HBM; MRAM is capacitorless, nonvolatile and ~3-4x denser than SRAM.

title: Shipping container: universal compressed-page format across all tiers
idea: Like the ISO container ending break-bulk cargo, standardize a 4 KB compressed-page envelope (codec ID, dictionary hash, size class, checksum) that CPUs, GPUs, CXL memory, NICs and SSDs read and write natively, so pages move between tiers and machines without decompress/recompress.
why: Recompression cost keeps compressed tiers small; a standard lets 30-50% of footprint stay compressed end-to-end (1.3-1.8x capacity).

title: Follow-the-moon: migrate memory-hungry batch jobs to night regions
idea: Imposed limit: no region may buy DRAM for its own daytime peak. Fleet schedulers move memory-heavy batch work (index builds, preemptible training, analytics) to regions whose interactive load is at its nightly low, and each region is sized for the global average instead of its local peak.
why: Daily swings in DRAM utilization run 30-50%; shifting work across time zones can cut fleet-installed DRAM ~15-25%.

title: Bit-plane storage with learned LSB synthesis on read
idea: IFR: store only the bits that matter. Closest: error-tolerant arrays (activations, images, sensor data) are stored as bit planes, MSB planes in DRAM and LSB planes dropped or parked in flash; on read a tiny predictor in the memory controller synthesizes dithered LSBs from neighbouring values within a programmer-declared SNR budget.
why: 1.5-2.5x capacity for media and ML activations at controlled error.

title: JPEG for the KV cache: DCT along the token axis
idea: Treat each attention head's K and V as an image (tokens x channels), apply a block DCT along the token axis where neighbouring tokens correlate, and quantize with per-head learned quantization tables like JPEG luminance tables; the attention kernel inverse-transforms blocks in SRAM.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory; transform coding before quantization claims 4-8x smaller KV at <1% quality loss vs ~2-4x for plain quantization.

title: Printed battery laminate makes DRAM durable, killing write buffers
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a printed thin-film zinc battery laminated onto each module powers a flush to onboard flash on power loss, making the DRAM itself durable. Databases and filesystems can then drop their separate write-ahead-log buffers and duplicate caches, because the primary copy in DRAM is already safe.
why: Durable DRAM removes duplicate buffering (WAL buffers, page cache alongside app cache) worth ~10-20% of database host memory, with no supercap bank.

title: Price-indexed scheduler decides park versus re-prefill for idle sessions
idea: IFR: idle conversations hold no memory yet resume instantly. Closest: the serving scheduler compares each parked session's KV cost (GB x expected idle seconds x spot DRAM $/GB-s) with the FLOP cost of re-prefilling from text, using a learned per-user think-time distribution, and evicts to text or flash whenever re-prefill is cheaper.
why: 30-60% of inference KV belongs to sessions idle between turns; with DRAM at 4x price this cuts provisioned KV DRAM ~2x by turning abundant compute into memory.

title: Transcendent memory, fixed: rack-pooled ephemeral page cache over CXL switch
idea: Linux cleancache/frontswap were deleted because only Xen used them and copies were synchronous per hypervisor. Rebuild tmem's put/get-may-fail semantics on a CXL 3 switch-attached rack pool with async DMA: hosts push clean page-cache pages to the pool and drop them locally, and the pool may discard anything anytime, so no coherence or durability is needed.
why: Hosts stop overprovisioning page cache; ~20-30% less DRAM per server since clean data is held once per rack and can be dropped safely.

title: Minify host memory: attention computed inside the SSD
idea: Minify host memory for long-context KV by keeping it on SSDs whose controllers include attention engines. The host sends queries and receives only softmax-weighted outputs (KBs), so the bulk KV never crosses PCIe.
why: Long-context KV moves to NAND at ~1/15 the cost per bit: >=10x capacity at the same cost, and data movement drops too.

title: Voyager's 69 kilobytes: compact bytecode tier for cold server code
idea: From Voyager's tiny memory and threaded interpretive code: toolchains emit server binaries as dense bytecode for the ~90% of code that is cold and native code only for profiled hot paths; a threaded interpreter runs the cold code, shrinking resident text segments.
why: Cold code is 5-10x smaller as bytecode; for microservice fleets with hundreds-of-MB binaries, code DRAM falls ~10x with matching fab-water savings.

title: Approximate MLC storage, fixed: precision-tiered flash cells for KV
idea: Sampson et al.'s approximate MLC storage never shipped because general files cannot tolerate errors. KV caches can: write sign/exponent/high-mantissa bits to SLC-mode pages and low-mantissa bits to QLC-mode pages with relaxed program-verify, raising density and cutting program time for the error-tolerant bits.
why: Offloaded KV in flash at ~2x density with faster writes, so no DRAM is needed for cold KV beyond a small working window.

title: Texture-compression units serve as free neural-weight decompressors
idea: Combine GPU fixed-function texture block decoders (ASTC/BC7 endpoints-plus-indices) with weight storage: quantize weight matrices into 4x4 blocks fitted with learned endpoints, store them as compressed textures, and fetch through the texture path straight into the tensor-core operand feed.
why: 3-5 bits per weight with zero added decode logic or ALU cost, cutting HBM capacity spent on weights 3-5x versus BF16.

title: Allocation-time hash-consing of immutable values in managed runtimes
idea: Box: dedup × runtime allocator × immutable object × at allocation × concurrent table of canonical instances. Strings, tuples, boxed numbers, decoded JSON subtrees and records marked immutable are looked up on allocation and replaced by a canonical shared instance.
why: Data-heavy services carry 20–40% duplicate immutable objects; canonicalization reclaims most of it in software, with no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Cross-finetune KV sharing below the first modified layer
idea: Imposed limit: a system prompt's KV may be stored once across all model variants. The platform requires finetunes to freeze the bottom k layers; those layers' KV is then bit-identical to the base model's, so every variant shares one prefix-KV store for the frozen layers and keeps private KV only for the layers it changed.
why: Serving hundreds of finetunes duplicates prefix KV; sharing the frozen layers' KV cuts that 2-5x, depending on how many layers are frozen.

title: Expert homing: move tokens to experts, never copy experts
idea: Imposed limit: each mixture-of-experts expert may exist in DRAM exactly once across the fleet. Experts are pinned to home nodes, and tokens (a few KB of activations each) travel over the network to the expert's home, batched across many requests to amortize the hops.
why: Copying every expert into every replica multiplies weight DRAM by the replica count; homing keeps weight DRAM constant as replicas grow, potentially 10-100x less in large fleets, at the cost of network traffic.

title: Row-buffer-sized compression blocks exploiting 8 KB overfetch
idea: DRAM activates an 8 KB row anyway, so compress at row granularity, using large-window LZ/BDI with a per-row dictionary. A row-buffer-side engine on the buffer chip or base die decompresses, while the CPU still sees 64 B lines. Compression moves up from line scale to row scale, so the overfetch becomes a free large window.
why: Large blocks compress 1.5-2x better than 64 B lines, for 1.8-2.5x effective capacity. It also puts the 128x overfetch (fact 8) to use.

title: Charge-domain KV attention in glass capacitor arrays
idea: Attention needs dot products, not exactly stored bits. Store each key as analog voltages on TFT capacitors on glass (3-4 effective bits per cell), compute q.k by switched-capacitor charge sharing along the columns, digitize only the top-k scores, and fetch the values for those tokens digitally.
why: The KV cache moves off silicon DRAM into cheap glass area as approximate storage: ~4x fewer bits than FP16, and no KV traffic during the score phase.

title: Byte-second pricing for compilers, runtimes and schedulers
idea: Allocators, ML compilers and cluster schedulers optimize byte-seconds (capacity x residency time) instead of peak bytes. The compiler rematerializes or streams any tensor whose recompute energy is lower than the cost of holding it in DRAM for that many byte-seconds, and clusters bill tenants per GB-microsecond actually resident.
why: Moving the metric from space to space x time makes short-lived data cheap and idle long-held data expensive. That gives 2-5x less activation footprint in training and 20-30% at cluster level.

title: SONOS NOR arrays compute dense layers where the weights sit
idea: IFR: weights never move and never occupy DRAM. Closest within Si/O/N: poly-Si/SiO2/Si3N4/SiO2 charge-trap NOR arrays (no Hf, W or Ta; Ti-silicide contacts) store 4-bit weights as trapped charge and do analog multiply-accumulate by summing bitline currents; only activations and KV use DRAM.
why: Removes weight DRAM (50-80% of inference memory) with a three-element memory stack mature U.S. fabs already run.

title: Minify parameters, magnify retrieval from a flash corpus
idea: Minify the parametric model ~10-25x and magnify non-parametric memory: knowledge sits in a NAND-resident retrieval corpus that the model queries per chunk, RETRO-style, so DRAM holds only the small model and a hot shard.
why: Weight DRAM falls >=10x for equal quality, with facts moved to bits that cost ~1/15 as much.

title: Ternary weights packed five trits per byte with LUT decode
idea: Box: representation shrink × model training × weights × train time × 3^5 = 243 states in 8 bits + table decode. Models trained natively ternary store five weights per byte and decode via a 256-entry table held in registers or shared memory.
why: 1.6 bits per weight versus 16 is a 10× weight-memory cut, achieved with algorithms and existing GPUs only, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Temporal mipmap KV cache with on-demand full-resolution recall
idea: Attention K/V is stored as a pyramid over token time. The last ~2k tokens stay at full resolution. Older spans are pooled into 8- and 64-token summary vectors that stay in HBM, while their full-resolution copies are parked in flash. When a query puts more than a threshold of attention mass on a summary, the controller fetches that span at full resolution for the next step, like texture mipmapping applied to time.
why: Resident KV grows roughly logarithmically instead of linearly with context, needing 5-10x less HBM at 128k-1M tokens while the detail that is needed can still be recalled.

title: Tardigrade vitrification swaps idle KV cache for token transcript
idea: When a chat session goes idle, its multi-GB KV cache is 'desiccated' to the token transcript plus a 1-2% anchor subset of KV states; on return the session is rehydrated by parallel prefill seeded from the anchors, like a tardigrade reviving from its tun state.
why: Inference capacity: idle sessions hold ~1000x less memory, so 5-10x more concurrent sessions per GB.

title: Argon's idleness: old KV distilled into a fixed recurrent state
idea: Argon means lazy; every 4k tokens a linear-attention distiller head folds the oldest KV block into a fixed per-layer state matrix of a few MB, so decoding attends to a sliding window plus the state instead of reading the whole KV cache.
why: At 128k context, per-token memory reads fall from the full KV (GBs) to window plus state, >10x lower memory energy per generated token, and KV capacity stays flat as context grows (energy, density).

title: Switch multicast streams one shared weight copy to all GPUs
idea: Combine a pooled weight store (CXL/NVLink memory node) with switch-level multicast: data-parallel replicas run in lockstep and the switch broadcasts each layer's weights just in time to every GPU, which keeps only a two-layer ring buffer instead of a full replica in HBM.
why: HBM spent on duplicated weights falls by the replica count (8-64x), freeing it for KV cache or allowing smaller-HBM parts (fact 6).

title: Universal genetic code standard for portable compressed pages
idea: Every organism reads the same genetic code; an open, versioned compressed-page format lets a page compressed on one vendor's module move bit-for-bit to another's during repair or recycling without decompression or vendor lock-in.
why: Keeps 2-3x effective capacity intact across hardware swaps and makes compression tiers repairable.

title: Bone remodeling rotates hot rows to equalize aging stress
idea: Osteoclasts and osteoblasts continuously rebuild stressed bone; the controller migrates hot pages across banks and ranks on a slow schedule so hammer exposure, BTI aging and thermal stress spread evenly, leaving each chip with uniform, predictable remaining life that makes reuse grading simple.
why: Longer first life and higher reuse yield; fewer modules scrapped early from localized wear.

title: Minify KV to token IDs; magnify recompute on idle FLOPs
idea: Minify cold context from ~160-320 KB of K/V per token to its 4-byte token ID. Keep only sink tokens and a hot window resident, and rematerialize K/V for older spans by chunked re-prefill on idle tensor cores when attention scores route there.
why: Trades abundant FLOPs for scarce bits: >=10x (up to 1000x) smaller KV footprint on the same hardware, so no added cost.

title: Looped transformers reuse one block's weights many times
idea: Inverts 'each layer needs its own weights': models are retrained or distilled into a few shared blocks that execute repeatedly, with tiny per-iteration adapters, so depth costs FLOPs on existing GPUs instead of weight bytes.
why: Weight memory drops 4-12x for the same effective depth, freeing DRAM/HBM for KV and larger batches.

title: Oxide-TFT leakage as a built-in forgetting curve for KV
idea: For most heads, attention decays with distance, so old tokens can fade instead of being refreshed. Store low-priority KV heads on glass TFT capacitors whose leakage is tuned per bank (channel length, gate bias) to a chosen time constant, and have the sense circuit treat faded entries as zero.
why: Zero refresh energy and automatic eviction with no bookkeeping; these heads, roughly 30-50% of KV in long-context models, need no silicon DRAM at all.

title: SoftRAM 95 lesson: audited effective-GB rating for memory compression
idea: Syncronys' SoftRAM 95 sold 'RAM doubling' that did nothing, poisoning trust in memory compression for decades. Create an independent, FTC-backed certification that measures delivered effective GB on standard workload traces, so OEMs can sell and procurement can count 'certified 1.6x effective memory' with smaller physical DRAM.
why: Demand-side supply: if buyers trust 1.5-2x compressed capacity, DRAM content per laptop/phone/server can drop 25-40% during the shortage.

title: 2050 engineer laughing at boxed integers: unboxed CPython containers
idea: A 2050 engineer finds 28-byte Python ints absurd. A CPython extension, later an upstream PEP, gives lists and dicts lazily specialized storage: a container holding only ints, floats or short ASCII strings switches to a packed unboxed array or arena and boxes values only on access, invisibly to user code. Two core developers, 24 months.
why: Python data-processing heaps are 4-10x the raw data size. Specialized containers cut DRAM 2-5x in ETL jobs, ML data loaders and web caches.

title: Thirty-year spares mindset: retired DIMMs reborn as CXL memory
idea: From industrial operators who stock spares for decades: decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs are tested, binned and slotted into CXL Type-3 expander boxes with per-DIMM health maps and stronger ECC, serving as the warm tier that new DRAM would otherwise fill.
why: Reused bits need zero new wafer starts, so their manufacturing water is ~0 (far beyond 10x), while supply grows by the fleet's retirement volume.

title: Embossed holographic film stores frozen prefix KV caches
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): the KV caches of high-traffic frozen prefixes (system prompts, popular documents, codebases) are mastered once per model release as computer-generated surface-relief holograms and copied by roll-to-roll embossing, the process used for credit-card holograms. An LED-addressed reader projects a whole KV page onto a photodiode array in one flash.
why: Shared-prefix KV is read-only yet duplicated across GPUs; moving it to film that costs pennies per copy frees DRAM/HBM for per-user KV, ~1.5-3x more sessions per accelerator.

title: Halftone error diffusion: 2-3-bit stored activations preserving dot products
idea: Borrowed from Floyd-Steinberg print halftoning: when activations or KV are written to memory at 2-3 bits, each element's rounding error is diffused into its not-yet-quantized neighbors along the reduction dimension, so downstream dot products stay nearly unbiased. A small write-path unit performs the diffusion in the store stream.
why: 5-8x fewer bits than FP16 for stored intermediates with accuracy closer to naive 4-6-bit quantization; direct capacity and bandwidth gain.
